beats.heading: Walker opening
beats.narration_text: Hello — this is Liam, in for Bear. The ask: three simple 3D props for a 2D cave game, built by Claude inside a running Blender, then checked in Godot.

props.segment: Cold Stone, Warm Gold: Three 3D Props for a Cave Mage

beats.heading: What got built
beats.narration_text: Three 3D props for a 2D cave game. The check passed: the size is right. Whether they also look right is a different question — and only a person can answer it.

props.text:
Three 3D props
for a 2D cave game.
The check passed:
the look is right.

beats.heading: The assignment, and this game
beats.narration_text: The game is walker magic: a pixel-art fire mage in a cold cave, so far all 2D. Assignment three asks for three props from basic shapes — at most six shapes and five hundred triangles each — through the Blender MCP, with one edit by hand, a small Godot scene, and a headless check. The rock is a roadblock she jumps. The crystal is cold-blue decoration. The chest is the reward at the exit, warm on purpose: in this cave, warmth means fire made it safe.

beats.heading: Learning the window
beats.narration_text: Before any build prompt, the author measured Blender's shapes in Scene Statistics. A default UV sphere: 960 triangles, nearly twice the limit. An ico sphere at one subdivision: 20. A six-sided cone: 10. Those readings became the predictions: sixty triangles for the rock, thirty for the crystal, seventy-six for the chest.

beats.heading: The prompt and the approval
beats.narration_text: Each asset began with a written prompt and a plan. This is the rock's: build only this asset, exactly as the brief specifies, and don't export yet. Claude Code proposed six steps, and nothing ran until the author pressed Yes, build it.

beats.heading: Rock, Revision 1 (code)
beats.narration_text: This is the revised rock, call R2. Each stone's turns are baked into its mesh, so its rotation stays zero; then its scale is the target size divided by what its vertices actually measure.

beats.heading: Rock (result)
beats.narration_text: The first build sized the stones from a looser box. The final fit had to stretch the rock 1.19 times wide, and it read as three dice. Sized from the vertices, Revision 1 fits with factors of exactly one. One flaw stays: a 6.6-centimetre gap at the floor between the base stones, accepted as a known limitation.

beats.heading: The hand edit
beats.narration_text: The crystal carries the hand edit. The first three attempts never reached the scene; Claude Code re-measured and saw no change. The fourth stuck: Crystal Short B, rotation Z typed as twenty degrees, Enter, and an asterisk in the title bar.

beats.heading: Crystal (code)
beats.narration_text: That turn narrowed the crystal to 32 centimetres, under the brief. Call J1 doesn't stretch it: it lengthens only that cone along its own axis, so the rotation stays exactly as typed.

beats.heading: Crystal (result)
beats.narration_text: A factor of 1.21. The crystal is back to 35 by 35 by 60 centimetres and thirty triangles, with the hand-turned cone still leaning where it was put.

beats.heading: Chest lid (code)
beats.narration_text: The chest lid is an eight-sided cylinder on its side, turned until one face points straight up. Line 134 then asks one question: does the true top reach 0.6 metres?

beats.heading: Chest (result)
beats.narration_text: It does: 0.600, flat. An eight-sided lid as deep as the body rises half its depth, so the split came out 37.6 plus 22.4 centimetres instead of 35 plus 25. The total held, and the brief records the change.

beats.heading: Export (code)
beats.narration_text: Export uses Blender's own G-L-T-F exporter: binary, plus-Y up, the default in 5.2.2, with materials.

beats.heading: Export (result)
beats.narration_text: Read back outside Blender, each file has one node with no transform, height on Y starting at zero, and exactly the predicted triangles. The chest's lock reaches plus-Z: its front faces the camera, as the brief predicted.

beats.heading: The author's look in Godot
beats.narration_text: Then the author's own look in Godot: from the game camera, from above, from below through the floor. All three stand upright with closed undersides, and the chest's gold, lowered to metallic 0.3, reads yellow-gold. But the background was Godot's default grey, the floor's edges showed, and from the side the mage became a thin line.

beats.heading: The scene fixes (code)
beats.narration_text: Two fixes in the scene file: a WorldEnvironment with the cave's background colour, and billboard mode on the mage, so she turns to face the camera. Her pixel size, 0.0227 metres, makes sixty-four pixels exactly 1.45 metres.

beats.heading: The running scene (result)
beats.narration_text: Here it is running, at native 4K, with a scripted camera. The props stand on the floor beside a 1.45-metre mage. As the camera swings behind them, she keeps facing us — a flat sprite always shows her front — and with one light from the front, the rock and the chest go almost black, while the crystal keeps its blue.

beats.heading: The headless check (code)
beats.narration_text: The headless check loads each file, measures its true vertex bounds, and compares them with numbers copied from the brief, within two centimetres.

beats.heading: The headless check (result)
beats.narration_text: Twenty-two checks, zero failures. It can fail, too: with the rock's width changed to 1.1 in a scratch copy, it reported one failure and exit code one. What it can't tell you is whether these read as a rock, a crystal and a chest, or how the glow looks in a real cave.

beats.heading: What Claude got wrong
beats.narration_text: Claude got things wrong. It sized the first rock from an overstated box. When the hand edit didn't appear, it blamed a different Blender; it was the same one, and the rotation was probably cancelled. It once said FRICTIONAL dot M D didn't exist. Each was caught by checking, not by trust.

beats.heading: Verdict
beats.narration_text: The verdict. Built: three props through the MCP, their files, a prop room and a check. Measured: size, origin, transforms, triangles and colours. Judged by the author: that they read as what they are. Still unknown: how the floor gap and the glow look in real play. Claude Code wrote the Blender code, the scene and the check; Claude in chat proposed sizes and colours, drafted the build prompts, and drafted documents; the author chose, approved, edited by hand, and looked. Source shown: commit 8 d 8 8 9 5 c.

beats.heading: Your Turn
beats.narration_text: Your turn. Please use Walker to add a torch beside my treasure chest: one prop from basic shapes, under 150 triangles, warm emission, origin at its base. Before building, predict its bounding box in metres, then add a line to my headless asset check that fails if the prediction is wrong. The torch is the brief's next step: warmth beside the chest. The prediction comes first, so the check can prove you wrong. Take this prompt, run it on your own game, and change one thing. Liam, in for Bear.
